grammar.title: Grammar
grammar.rule: ふだが｜ひとつ｜あります。めいのふだ｜と｜れんのふだです。

tables.caption: Two people; two cards
rows: ふうとうのなかをみます

grammar.note_en:
This chapter counts ordinary objects with ひとつ (one), ふたつ (two) and みっつ (three). In ふうとうのなかにめいのふだがひとつあります, “There is one tag belonging to Mei inside the envelope,” the number gives the quantity of tags. In ふだはふたつあります, “There are two tags,” は keeps the tags as the topic. The story also identifies the set being counted with a nominal predicate, as in ふだはみっつです, “There are three tags / the tags number three.” Do not treat the counter as a plural ending attached to a noun. The words for envelope, tag and box keep their written shapes.

ひとつ/ふたつ/みっつ form one common general counting series for things. They are not the Japanese way to count people, and they do not replace every specialised counter. Flat sheets and cards often use a more specific counter, which will be taught later. Here the bounded general counter lets you follow sets of physical tags and small objects without learning that later counter. Preserve the small っ in みっつ; みつ is not the same spelling.

A quantity can also identify a set before a noun: みっつのふだ means “the three tags.” In ゆいはみっつのふだをみます, “Yui looks at the three tags,” the number identifies everything she is comparing. She is not saying that all three belong in the envelope. The entire visible set has three cards, while the intended envelope set has two. That difference matters to the story.

と links nouns in an explicit pair or list. めいとれん means “Mei and Ren”; めいのふだとれんのふだ means “Mei’s tag and Ren’s tag.” と does not mean that the two things are identical, and it is not a general word for joining any two sentences. In this chapter ふうとうのなまえは「めい」と「れん」です means “The names on the envelope are Mei and Ren.” Those names tell the volunteers which pair belongs together. ゆいとれんはいっしょにふうとうのなかをみます means “Yui and Ren look inside the envelope together.” The familiar に in いっしょに belongs to the taught whole expression “together”; it is not naming a physical location there.

おおきさ means size. おおきさはおなじです means “The size is the same.” なまえはちがいます means “The names differ.” Mei and Ren have distinct cards with different names; their matching size does not make them one physical card. Their reverse sides carry copies of the same reading-room photograph. おなじしゃしん means “the same photograph” in that sense of matching printed images, not that a single piece of paper has somehow moved between both cards. おなじ precedes the noun directly here: おなじおおきさ. Do not add な to that phrase.

うら is the reverse or back of a flat thing. ふだのうらにしゃしんがあります means “There is a photograph on the reverse of the card.” Turning a card over does not create another card. Its front and reverse still belong to one physical object. The delivered front/back diagrams show which card is being inspected; Mei and Ren’s matching small papers turn out to be しょうたいじょう, invitation cards. Yui’s larger name card is a separate item.

もうひとつ means one more or the other one in the two-item set being discussed. もうひとつはわたしのふだです means “The other one is my card.” The context identifies which set is meant; it is not a new name for every missing thing. When the right pair is together in the envelope, the counting problem is solved.

A らん is an entry field on a form. じかんのらん means “the time field.” It appears below the photograph on the invitation, and is visibly blank in the delivered close-up. The unfinished spoken じかんは……？ means “And the time…?” It is an ordinary elliptical question prompted by that blank, not a taught negative existential or a full when/what-time question. The chapter gives no meeting time. Do not supply one from your own imagination; the next chapter will address it. The final questions and their visible stage cues distinguish the opening, discovery and completed packet.

notes: Scratch draft for parent application only after chapter2 release. No code review or chapter certification is claimed.
Original modern Japanese kana narrative, no audio or quotation. Preserve all practice and the original narrative window.
One physical card has two sides; matching photograph copies and matching sizes are not identity of the physical cards. Yui’s large card remains outside the two-recipient envelope.
The insertion is shown through an actual delivered hand/card/envelope picture and resulting location, using only taught finite verbs. No new いれます or negative existential is assumed.
The time field is visibly blank, and the natural elliptical じかんは……？ carries the hook without an untaught full time question.
